title: Sovereignty, Agility, and Scale: How Enterprises in Asia Pacific are Redefining Modernization
summary: Discover how leading enterprises across Asia Pacific and the Middle East are using private cloud to modernize infrastructure, strengthen sovereignty, and accelerate AI adoption.
body_text: From Electronics to Banking: Inside the Infrastructure Transformations at Samsung Electronics, Vodafone Idea, and Taiwan's Leading Banks I've spent more than two decades sitting across the table from IT leaders around the world, and one truth remains constant: technology decisions are never really about technology. They are about people trying to keep a promise to their own customers: a bank guaranteeing a transaction, a telco keeping a network up, or an organization promising sovereignty over its most critical workloads. Lately, those promises are getting harder to keep, as enterprises race to put AI models to work inside their business. Beneath all that AI ambition lies real infrastructure complexity. Most teams are managing a patchwork of legacy systems, multiple vendors, and temporary fixes that were never designed to work together. A challenge that only multiplies as containerized workloads, Kubernetes, and frontier AI models become default requirements. Consider that Broadcom’s recent Private Cloud Outlook 2026 Report highlighted that 38% of enterprise IT leaders in APJ point to Kubernetes operations as their single biggest skills gap. Against this backdrop, I no longer judge modernization by how many workloads the infrastructure can run. Instead what I look for is whether the strategy is driven by a genuine business need, the chosen platform earns a CIO's trust, and whether the architecture gives developers the freedom to innovate while giving leadership complete operational and data sovereignty. The best way to demonstrate what that trust looks like is with the customers who are proving it every day. Samsung Electronics: Maximizing Developer Agility and Simplifying Kubernetes Operations by Running VMs and Containers on a Unified Private Cloud Platform Inside Samsung Electronics’ cloud platform team, engineers spent too much energy standing up the basics, such as wiring together Virtual Machines (VMs), Load Balancers (LBs), and Virtual Private Clouds (VPCs) before a single developer could start building anything. However, by adopting VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) and automating the infrastructure control plane, the team streamlined cluster orchestration and established an environment where internal development teams could easily access vital cluster-scoped resources, such as Custom Resource Definitions (CRDs). By moving to dedicated clusters built on our platform, Samsung Electronics gave every team the freedom to manage and upgrade their environment, on their own schedule, without waiting on anyone else. What makes Samsung Electronics’ approach stand out is that they didn't just patch a problem— they reengineered how their internal teams should experience infrastructure entirely. This infrastructure modernization served as a critical stepping stone toward securing the agility and control of a software-defined private cloud architecture. Samsung Electronics is now scaling that foundation with real confidence, and it's set to carry them into the next wave of AI, design, and manufacturing workloads. Vodafone Idea Limited: Overcoming Supply Chain Bottlenecks and Slashing Chipset Costs by up to 40% with VKS Another great customer example is Vodafone Idea Limited which runs VMs and containers on a unified private cloud platform. To support its nationwide 5G rollout—reaching 220 million customers across 133 cities—and modernize its critical CRM, billing, and inventory systems, Vodafone Idea launched its 'Pragati Transformation Project.' Built on VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) and VKS, the project unifies workloads across its environments. During deployment, global hardware supply chain disruptions and a 200% spike in hardware costs threatened to delay the project. By leveraging VKS, Vodafone bypassed these hurdles, creating independent, isolated kubernetes clusters within existing vSphere environments managed by partners. This separated software delivery timelines from underlying hardware constraints, allowing Vodafone Idea to deploy large production workloads, including 195 billing pods across eight namespaces, and saving three months on the transformation timeline. Today, Vodafone Idea expects to slash chipset costs by 30-40% using more NVMe infrastructure to offset the costs of expensive storage. This strategy improves infrastructure utilization by 30% and accelerates provisioning timelines by over 60% . Ultimately, it delivers a highly secure, AI-ready platform capable of sustaining rapid growth within budget. That's the kind of story that stays with me as I meet customers across the region. This is a team that refused to let a supply chain crisis become a customer-facing failure, maintaining full control over their deployment roadmap and coming out the other side stronger than before. Taiwan’s Leading Banks: Speed Without Regulatory Compromise In Taiwan’s financial sector, regulatory oversight is amongst the most stringent in the world. For institutions like Taishin Bank and First Commercial Bank, compliance, data residency, and operational resilience are non-negotiable. When both banks moved to unify their virtual machines and containerized workloads on a single private cloud platform, the objective was clear: accelerate digital services without compromising governance. Service provisioning workflows that previously took weeks of manual orchestration now take just hours. Most importantly, both institutions achieved this agility while maintaining total data sovereignty and satisfying their regulatory requirements. They proved that in banking, innovation and control do not have to be mutually exclusive. Investing in an Architecture You Can Trust If there is one common thread that connects Samsung Electronics, Vodafone Idea, and Taiwan's leading banks, it isn't the technology stack. None of them modernized because they wanted infrastructure that could run more workloads. They modernized because they wanted sovereignty, choice and control over their data and an architecture they could trust. In every case, that trust was built on the same underlying decision: moving away from siloed environments and onto a single, unified private cloud platform capable of supporting VMs, containers, and AI workloads. To all our customers and partners embarking on this journey: thank you for trusting us with your infrastructure and partnering with us to modernize it for the future. About the Author About the Author Sylvain Cazard President, Asia Pacific and Japan, Broadcom

title: Currents: Rebecca Rose, Samsung, POAP and more news Welcome to the OpenSea digest. Let’s look back through the biggest NFT and web3 news of the week. 8.7.2026
summary: Welcome to the OpenSea digest. Let’s look back through the biggest NFT and web3 news of the week.
body_text: Welcome to the OpenSea digest. Let’s look back through the biggest NFT and web3 news of the week. Rebecca Rose's "Popol Vuh" debuts at Mexico City's Anahuacalli Museum Digital artist Rebecca Rose 's animated piece "Popol Vuh" debuts this weekend at the Museo Diego Rivera Anahuacalli in Mexico City, as part of 8NAP Art 's Digital Encounters exhibition, she said in an X post . The artwork revisits a moment from painter Diego Rivera's life, when he released his watercolor collection into the wild as an act of letting go, Rose wrote. Ahead of the debut, Rose said art collector Benny, known online as Redbeard , acquired the piece in a private sale. She credited his advocacy for digital art and his ties to the community, noting she first met him at in-person NFT events where he spoke on panels. Proud to announce “Popol Vuh” was collected by @redbeardnft via private acquisition! True art patrons support culture in every space they inhabit, and Benny champions the arts not just through collecting, but through every day advocacy and community connection. Couldn't be more… pic.twitter.com/j9x94QLSmD — Rebecca Rose (@RebeccaRose) August 3, 2026 Blockchain game studio Proof of Play shuts down, open-sources its code Proof of Play , the game studio behind pirate-themed blockchain game Pirate Nation , announced Aug. 4 it is shutting down. The company said it aimed to prove blockchain gaming could power a new decentralized internet, but it couldn't build a business to support the idea at scale. Proof of Play is open-sourcing its code, including the Pirate Nation Unity app and smart contracts , and releasing its artwork, logos, and Founder Pirates NFT collection under a CC0 license, a public copyright waiver letting anyone reuse the work without permission. The Pirate Nation Foundation , a separate group, will keep supporting the project's $PIRATE token. Another Proof of Play game, Shiba Story Go! , sold to a third party and will keep running independently. Proof of Play will be ceasing operations. When we started out, we believed games using blockchain tech had the potential to usher in a new, decentralized internet. Ultimately, we couldn't build a product and sustainable business that proved out this thesis at scale. We are… — Proof of Play (@ProofOfPlay) August 4, 2026 Samsung plans to add stablecoins to Samsung Wallet on hundreds of millions of Galaxy phones Samsung revealed plans to add stablecoin support, a type of cryptocurrency designed to hold a steady value by tying itself to the U.S. dollar, to Samsung Wallet. During its Galaxy Unpacked event on July 22, Samsung reportedly showed a mockup wallet balance labeled $USDC, but has not yet confirmed whether it has an official partnership with Circle, $USDC ’s issuer, nor a launch date or which blockchain network the stablecoin will run on. POAP, the digital attendance badge platform, is shutting down after five years POAP , the blockchain company known for turning event attendance into digital collectibles, is winding down, co-founder Isabel Gonzalez announced Aug. 3. Since launching at a Denver hackathon in 2019, POAP minted nearly 7.6 million badges for more than 46,000 organizers, according to the platform's figures. In her announcement, Gonzalez pointed to collaborations with organizations including American Express, Warner Music Group, and Bayer. “POAP meant something to a lot of people,” said Gonzalez. She added that crypto's funding patterns have made it hard to build a lasting business without compromising what made POAP meaningful in the first place. The company has not set a final shutdown date. The badges live permanently on public blockchains, so collectors will be able to keep their tokens regardless of what happens to POAP 's company. Access to the company's website, gallery and supporting tools remains uncertain long term. After 5+ years, we're winding down POAP. Over the years, we: * minted millions of collectibles across hundreds of communities. * did incredible collaborations with world-class organizations - Coinbase, Amex, WMG, Bayer, and a long tail of others, including countless in crypto.… pic.twitter.com/iFbRqs5qsI — isabel (@izonline) August 3, 2026 Wells Fargo will launch tokenized deposits for corporate clients this fall Wells Fargo plans to launch tokenized deposits this fall, letting corporate and commercial clients eventually move money around the clock instead of waiting on standard banking hours, the bank said in an Aug. 4 announcement. Tokenized deposits turn customer funds into digital tokens on a blockchain , a shared digital ledger that records transactions, so the bank can settle payments nearly continuously while keeping the money inside the regulated banking system. The pilot program will start with U.S. dollar to British pound transfers on Wells Fargo's own blockchain platform, and Chief Financial Officer Mike Santomassimo called the launch a step forward for the bank's payment options. Wells Fargo plans to add more clients, countries and currencies through 2027, and the move follows a March trademark filing for WFUSD, a wordmark analysts read as a possible tokenized-deposit or stablecoin brand. Immutable launched a Seven Deadly Sins NFT adventure Blockchain platform Immutable opened its Seven Deadly Sins NFT Adventure on July 30, giving players a free mint according to a post from the company on X. Players complete quests within the game and reportedly earn web3 rewards through MARBLEX , a blockchain gaming platform. Immutable runs as a layer two network, a system built on top of Ethereum that processes transactions separately to cut costs and boost speed, and it uses zero-knowledge rollups, a method that bundles transactions off the main Ethereum network before confirming them, to keep minting and trading free of gas fees. The Seven Deadly Sins NFT Adventure is LIVE! Your ticket to an iconic 55M+ selling anime universe, built for epic quests and real Web3 rewards on @MARBLEXofficial And today’s main event… The 7DS Free Mint is officially OPEN! Jump into the journey, clear the gameplay quests,… — Immutable (@Immutable) July 30, 2026 AI company Krea will host a webinar on training AI to match a brand's art style AI image platform Krea will host a webinar Aug. 12 to show other brands how to train a custom model on their own visual style, building on a case study the company published about its work with NFT collection Doodles . Doodles trained a custom LoRA on Krea's Krea 2 model to reproduce its signature look, after mainstream image models kept missing details like exact eye placement and palette colors. A LoRA is a smaller add-on model trained on a focused set of images, in this case based on Doodles' internal style guide. title: Charles River Laboratories Announces Second-Quarter 2026 Results
summary: WILMINGTON, Mass. --(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 5, 2026-- Charles River Laboratories International, Inc. (NYSE: CRL) today reported its results for the second quarter ended June 27, 2026. Key Highlights Reports second-quarter revenue of $1.00 billion, GAAP loss per share of $(0.03), and non-GAAP earnings
body_text: WILMINGTON, Mass.--(BUSINESS WIRE)--Aug. 5, 2026-- Charles River Laboratories International, Inc. (NYSE: CRL) today reported its results for the second quarter ended June 27, 2026. Key Highlights Reports second-quarter revenue of $1.00 billion, GAAP loss per share of $(0.03), and non-GAAP earnings per share of $3.02. Organic revenue growth of 0.1% reached the highest level since the third quarter of 2023. Non-GAAP operating margin increased 420 basis points on a sequential basis to 20.5%, while the GAAP operating margin was essentially flat on a sequential basis at 11.9%. Increases 2026 guidance for revenue and non-GAAP earnings per share. Organic revenue guidance increasing by 150 basis points and non-GAAP earnings per share guidance increasing by $0.25 at midpoint. Guidance increases primarily driven by improving demand trends in the DSA segment and better-than-expected performance in the Manufacturing segment. Repurchased $100 million of common stock in the second quarter at an average price of $174 per share to enhance shareholder value. To refine and further strengthen its portfolio, the Company completed the divestitures of certain European Discovery Services sites as well as the CDMO and Cell Solutions businesses in May 2026. To further deepen its client relationships, the Company has joined Eli Lilly's TuneLab AI/ML platform by providing non-clinical testing expertise to optimize drug discovery and advance R&D modernization efforts. Additionally, it has collaborated with Arovella Therapeutics to provide in vitro Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) services, which was added through the PathoQuest acquisition. This collaboration will accelerate progress towards Arovella's alternative cancer treatment approaches. To advance its modernization efforts, Charles River introduced an enhanced digital pathology solution to drive efforts to further digitize and automate the Company. This AI-enabled, end-to-end workflow will deliver improved study turnaround times and increased pathologist efficiency. Second-Quarter Results Revenue was $1.00 billion, a decrease of 2.7% from $1.03 billion in the second quarter of 2025. On an organic basis, revenue increased 0.1%, driven by revenue growth in the Manufacturing Solutions (Manufacturing) and Discovery and Safety Assessment (DSA) segments, offset by a decline in the Research Models and Services (RMS) segment. Organic revenue growth excludes the effect of acquisitions, divestitures, and foreign currency translation. In the second quarter of 2026, the GAAP operating margin was 11.9%, compared to 9.7% in the second quarter of 2025. The increase in the GAAP operating margin was primarily driven by the CDMO business, including lower accelerated amortization expense related to certain client relationships. The GAAP net loss available to common shareholders for the second quarter of 2026 was $(1.5) million, or $(0.03) per diluted share, compared to GAAP net income of $52.3 million, or $1.06 per diluted share for the same period in 2025. The decrease was principally due to a loss related to the CDMO and Cell Solutions divestiture totaling $63.7 million, or $1.40 per share. On a non-GAAP basis, the second-quarter operating margin decreased to 20.5% from 22.1% in the second quarter of 2025, primarily as a result of higher study-related direct costs in the DSA segment and higher unallocated corporate costs. Non-GAAP net income was $146.2 million for the second quarter of 2026, a decrease of 5.0% from $154.0 million for the same period in 2025. Second-quarter diluted earnings per share on a non-GAAP basis were $3.02, a decrease of 3.2% from $3.12 per share in the second quarter of 2025. The non-GAAP net income and earnings per share decreases were driven primarily by the lower operating margin. The earnings per share decrease was partially offset by investment gains associated with the Company's deferred compensation plan, which totaled a net benefit of $0.19 per share in the second quarter. Birgit Girshick, Chief Executive Officer, said, "We made excellent progress in the second quarter on the execution of our Pathway to Purpose strategy. We are actively evaluating opportunities to modernize the Company and drive greater efficiency, to strengthen our leading drug development portfolio centered on regulated testing, and to further enhance our growth profile. We are focused on continuing to move forward on achieving our strategic initiatives and financial goals, which will strengthen our foundation and underpin our future success." "We were encouraged that the demand environment continued to strengthen in the second quarter, particularly for our DSA segment, as evidenced by the fact that we recorded the highest net book-to-bill in nearly four years. This improvement was broad based across our global biopharmaceutical and small and mid-sized biotechnology clients, and it is our goal to continue to capture additional share of our clients’ R&D spending by providing client-centric solutions and by leveraging our global scale and deep scientific expertise. As a result of our collective efforts, we delivered on our second-quarter financial targets – exceeding our prior outlook – and are raising our revenue and non-GAAP earnings per share guidance for the year," Ms. Girshick concluded. Second-Quarter Segment Results Research Models and Services (RMS) Revenue for the RMS segment was $209.5 million in the second quarter of 2026, a decrease of 1.8% from $213.3 million in the second quarter of 2025. Organic revenue decreased by 1.4%, due primarily to lower revenue for small research models in North America, as well as for research model services. The decline was partially offset by higher revenue for small research models in China. In the second quarter of 2026, the RMS segment’s GAAP operating margin increased to 17.3% from 16.8% in the second quarter of 2025, primarily due to lower amortization of intangible assets related to the sale of the Cell Solutions business. On a non-GAAP basis, the operating margin decreased to 24.5% from 25.3%. The non-GAAP operating margin decrease was primarily driven by the impact of lower sales volume and an unfavorable geographic revenue mix. Discovery and Safety Assessment (DSA) Revenue for the DSA segment was $606.5 million in the second quarter of 2026, a decrease of 1.9% from $618.0 million in the second quarter of 2025. Organic revenue increased by 0.2%, driven primarily by higher study volume for regulated safety assessment services. In the second quarter of 2026, the DSA segment’s GAAP operating margin increased to 20.5% from 19.9% in the second quarter of 2025. The increase was primarily driven by lower amortization of intangible assets related to the divestiture of certain European Discovery Services sites and lower third-party legal costs related to a non-human primate (NHP) supply matter. On a non-GAAP basis, the operating margin decreased to 25.6% from 27.4% in the second quarter of 2025. The non-GAAP operating margin decrease was primarily driven by higher study-related direct costs. Manufacturing Solutions (Manufacturing) Revenue for the Manufacturing segment was $188.1 million in the second quarter of 2026, a decrease of 6.3% from $200.8 million in the second quarter of 2025, primarily driven by the CDMO divestiture. Organic revenue increased 1.3%, driven primarily by higher revenue in the Microbial Solutions business. The Manufacturing segment’s GAAP operating margin was 34.9%, compared to 6.0% in the second quarter of 2025. On a non-GAAP basis, the operating margin increased to 37.8% from 32.8% in the second quarter of 2025. The GAAP and non-GAAP increases were driven primarily by the CDMO business, including the benefit from the divestiture. Stock Repurchase Update The Company repurchased 1.7 million shares for a total of $300.0 million during the year-to-date period ended June 27, 2026, including 0.6 million shares for a total of $100.0 million in the second quarter of 2026. As of June 27, 2026, the Company had $700.0 million remaining under its $1.0 billion stock repurchase authorization that was approved by the Board of Directors on October 29, 2025. 2026 Guidance Update The Company is increasing its 2026 revenue and non-GAAP earnings per share guidance, which was last updated on May 7, 2026. This increase primarily reflects the expected operational outperformance for the year, including in the second quarter, due primarily to improving demand trends in the DSA segment and better-than-expected performance in the Manufacturing segment. For the year, the Company expects the second-quarter investment gains associated with the deferred compensation plan will be largely offset by a higher tax rate, resulting in a negligible net impact to non-GAAP earnings per share. On a GAAP basis, the Company is reducing its earnings per share guidance due primarily to the net loss related to the divestitures. (4) These adjustments primarily include site consolidation (including site transition costs), severance, impairment, third-party consulting and professional services, and other costs related to the Company’s restructuring actions and efficiency initiatives. As a result of the resolution of the U.S. government investigations during fiscal year 2025, certain NHPs were subsequently utilized. Webcast Charles River has scheduled a live webcast on Wednesday, August 5, 2026, at 9:00 a.m. ET to discuss matters relating to this press release. To participate, please go to ir.criver.com and select the webcast link. You can also find the associated slide presentation and reconciliations of GAAP financial measures to non-GAAP financial measures on the website. Investor Day Charles River will host an Investor Day on Thursday, September 24, 2026, at 9:00 a.m. ET. The meeting will be webcast live on the Investor Relations section of the Company's website at ir.criver.com . Non-GAAP Reconciliations The Company reports non-GAAP results in this press release, which exclude often-one-time charges and other items that are outside of normal operations. A reconciliation of GAAP to non-GAAP results is provided in the schedules at the end of this press release. Use of Non-GAAP Financial Measures This press release contains non-GAAP financial measures, such as non-GAAP earnings per share, non-GAAP operating income, non-GAAP operating margin, and non-GAAP net income. Non-GAAP financial measures exclude, but are not limited to, the amortization of intangible assets and the purchase accounting step-up adjustment on inventory and certain long term biological assets, and other charges and adjustments related to our acquisitions and divestitures, including expenses associated with evaluating and integrating acquisitions and divestitures, including advisory fees, certain transition costs, and certain other transaction-related costs, as well as fair value adjustments associated with contingent consideration; charges, gains, and losses attributable to businesses or properties we plan to close, consolidate, or divest, including the divestitures of our CDMO and Cell Solutions businesses, the sale of certain of our European Discovery Services sites, and the sale of certain assets including real estate; severance and other costs associated with our restructuring initiatives; investment gains or losses associated with our venture capital and certain other strategic equity investments; certain legal costs and adjustments related to an NHP inventory charge in our DSA segment related to now concluded U.S. government investigations into the NHP supply chain; legal and advisory costs related to entering into a Cooperation Agreement with a shareholder; tax effect of all of the aforementioned matters; and adjustments related to the derecognition of certain deferred tax assets due to the CDMO Gene Therapy intangible asset impairment charge, the recognition of deferred tax assets expected to be utilized as a result of changes to the Company's international financing structure, and the revaluation of deferred tax liabilities as a result of foreign tax legislation. This press release also refers to our revenue on both a GAAP and non-GAAP basis: on a non-GAAP basis, we define “organic revenue growth” as reported revenue growth adjusted for foreign currency translation, acquisitions, and divestitures. We exclude these items from the non-GAAP financial measures because they are outside our normal operations. There are limitations in using non-GAAP financial measures, as they are not presented in accordance with generally accepted accounting principles, and may be different than non-GAAP financial measures used by other companies. In particular, we believe that the inclusion of supplementary non-GAAP financial measures in this press release helps investors to gain a meaningful understanding of our core operating results and future prospects without the effect of these often-one-time charges, and is consistent with how management measures and forecasts the Company's performance, especially when comparing such results to prior periods or forecasts. We believe that the financial impact of our acquisitions and divestitures (and in certain cases, the evaluation of such acquisitions and divestitures, whether or not ultimately consummated) is often large relative to our overall financial performance, which can adversely affect the comparability of our results on a period-to-period basis. In addition, certain activities and their underlying associated costs, such as business acquisitions, generally occur periodically but on an unpredictable basis. We calculate non-GAAP integration costs to include third-party integration costs incurred post-acquisition. Presenting revenue on an organic basis allows investors to measure our revenue growth exclusive of acquisitions, divestitures, and foreign currency exchange fluctuations more clearly. Non-GAAP results also allow investors to compare the Company’s operations against the financial results of other companies in the industry who similarly provide non-GAAP results. The non-GAAP financial measures included in this press release are not meant to be considered superior to or a substitute for results of operations presented in accordance with GAAP. The Company intends to continue to assess the potential value of reporting non-GAAP results consistent with applicable rules and regulations. title: Event Videography That Pays for Itself
summary: Event videography turns a one-day event into a year of marketing assets. The 2026 guide: planning, gear, costs, AI, and scaling at enterprise volume.
body_text: Creating Videos That Outlast Events Fireside chats are short-form gold for event videography — every soundbite cuts to a clip. You spent six months and a quarter of your annual marketing budget on a single two-day event. The keynote landed. The product demo got a standing ovation. Three of your biggest prospects flew in. And then the lights came up, the badges came off, and the moment was gone. ‍ The only thing left was whatever your event videographer captured. ‍ That is the entire premise of event videography in 2026. Live events are the most expensive marketing channel most companies still operate, and according to a Gartner 2025 CMO Spend Survey covered by Campaign , events command 19.3% of all offline marketing spend, the largest single offline allocation. Yet the asset that determines whether that spend keeps paying off long after the venue is empty is rarely treated like a strategic priority. It is treated like a line item. What Event Videography Is Event videography covers the dinners and after-parties, not just the keynote. Event videography is the art of capturing and editing social and special events onto video, covering everything except weddings. In practice, that catches a wide range: corporate conferences, product launches, charity galas, awards ceremonies, sports tournaments, concerts, brand activations, trade-show booths, panel discussions, executive keynotes, and even the social events around the main stage, like networking receptions and after-parties. ‍ What separates event videography from other forms of video production is constraint. There is no second take. The CEO walks the stage once. The product reveal happens at 7:42 PM, whether the camera is rolling or not. Every other genre of video is built around the assumption that you can reset and shoot again. Event videography is built around the assumption that you cannot. ‍ That single constraint reshapes everything downstream: gear has to be redundant, crews have to be rehearsed, audio has to be captured at multiple points, and post-production has to extract a story from whatever the cameras actually got. The best event videographers are not the ones with the best cameras. They are the ones with the best contingency plans. ‍ What used to be a nice-to-have wedding-video-adjacent service is now a core piece of B2B and B2C marketing infrastructure. Why Event Videography Earns Its Budget Back Every handshake on stage ends up in the recap reel — and in the email that sells next year. The headline question every CMO asks before signing off on event video coverage is the same: What does this actually return? The data has gotten dramatically better at answering it. ‍ Start with the macro picture. The Wyzowl 2026 video marketing survey, summarized at DigitalApplied, reports that 91% of businesses now use video as a marketing tool, up from 86% just two years earlier. Video has crossed the threshold from differentiator to default. Not having professional video coverage of your flagship event is, increasingly, the anomaly. ‍ The conversion case is even sharper. The same DigitalApplied analysis cites an 86% lift in landing page conversion when video is added and a 65% increase in email click-through rate when video is embedded. Apply that to a post-event campaign that goes out to thousands of attendees and prospects, and the math starts to look unambiguous. Where the event video actually outperforms The most underappreciated stat in this category comes from Wistia's 2026 State of Video Report, which analyzed over 13 million videos across 79 million hours of viewing data. The finding: videos placed on event pages saw the highest engagement rate of any page type on a website, beating product pages, homepages, and blog posts. ‍ The reason is intuitive once stated. Visitors who land on an event page have already self-selected as interested. Putting a sizzle reel from last year's edition in front of them is the lowest-friction conversion mechanism a marketing team can deploy. ‍ LinkedIn engagement reinforces the same pattern at the social layer. eMarketer reported in January 2026 that paid video ads on LinkedIn grew 30% year over year, fueled by short-form content. The B2B audience is now actively seeking the kind of authentic, in-the-room footage that only event videography can provide. Why the spend math actually works Take a $250,000 industry conference and budget $20,000 for a two-camera event video crew with editing. That 8% cost rider produces, conservatively: one 90-second sizzle reel, ten 30-to-60-second social cuts, three speaker keynote replays, a recap email video, a sales-enabled product demo segment, and B-roll for the next twelve months of content. ‍ If that bundle of assets adds even one closed deal, the ROI on the video specifically is usually multiples of the spend. If it powers a year of content marketing on top, it ranks among the most leveraged dollars on the marketing spreadsheet. ‍ That same logic underpins how Snappr customers think about visual content more broadly. As we explored how professional photography helped Renters Warehouse increase inquiries by 10x , the right visual asset, bought once, yields returns measured in inquiry volume for years. Pre-Production: Where Great Event Videos Are Made The pros mark the floor days before the doors open. The amateurs find out on the day itself. Most amateurs think the shoot is where the work happens. The professionals know the shoot is where the planning gets executed. Here is the pre-production sequence that the best crews run for every event. Step 1: Define the deliverables before you define anything else The single biggest mistake teams make is hiring an event videographer and then deciding what they want afterward. The shot list, gear, crew size, audio plan, and edit timeline all flow from the deliverables. A 60-second hype reel for Instagram needs a completely different shoot than a one-hour replay-quality keynote recording. ‍ Start by listing every video asset you want out of this event. A typical corporate event deliverable list might look like this: - One 90-second sizzle reel for social and the next event's landing page - Eight to twelve 30-second clips for LinkedIn and short-form social - Full-length recordings of three keynote sessions for replay and sales enablement - A two-minute customer story video featuring three on-site interviews - A three-minute recap video for the post-event email blast - B-roll library for the next twelve months of marketing content ‍ Once that list is locked, every other pre-production decision becomes downstream of it. Step 2: Walk the venue Never shoot an event you have not seen. A venue walk identifies sightlines for cameras, power outlets, lighting conditions at different times of day, the locations of the audio mixing board, the green room, the sponsor booth, and the bar for the reception, as well as where you can stash gear safely between sessions. This is also where you find the surprises the venue forgot to mention, like the giant pillar in the middle of the main hall, or the fact that the room dims for video segments. Step 3: Build the shot list and schedule A useful shot list is timestamped against the event schedule. For each session, the list specifies which cameras are where, who is operating them, what they capture, and which audio source they pull from. The same goes for non-session moments: registration, networking breaks, the keynote walk-on, the standing ovation, candid shots of attendees, and sponsor booth visits. ‍ The crews that consistently deliver are the ones who treat the shot list as a living document, updating it the day before based on the venue walk and the day of based on the run-of-show. Step 4: Brief the speakers and stakeholders Every speaker on camera gets a one-page briefing: when to expect the camera, where to look, mic check time, and a permission release on file. Every stakeholder who might appear (CEO, customer, sponsor) gets the same. This avoids the deeply unproductive moment when the C-suite finds out about the camera ten seconds before they are on it. Step 5: Confirm the contingency plan What happens if a camera fails? What happens if the venue's audio feed dies? What happens if the keynote runs forty minutes long? What happens if the headline speaker cancels? The pros war-game these before the event, not during. Capturing the Event: Coverage, Composition, and B-Roll By the time the doors open, the shoot becomes execution. Three principles separate professional event coverage from amateur footage. Multi-camera coverage is non-negotiable A single-camera event shoot is a recipe for unusable footage. The minimum professional configuration for a keynote-style session is three cameras: a locked-off wide on a tripod showing the full stage, a medium on the speaker tracking their movement, and a roaming third camera capturing audience reactions, slide pickups, and cinematic angles. Without the third camera, the edit feels static. Without the wide, you have no establishing shot. Without the medium, you have no usable footage of the speaker. ‍ For panels with multiple speakers, add a fourth camera or be prepared to whip the medium between participants. B-roll is what makes the edit feel like an event The keynote itself is the spine of the recap. B-roll is what gives it texture. Plan for thirty minutes of B-roll across registration, networking, sponsor booths, hallway energy, attendee close-ups, the room filling up, the standing ovation, branded signage, and the venue exterior. The team at Bull and Wolf put it cleanly in their event production guide: every event has a narrative arc; find it and follow it. The B-roll you shoot during the day is the connective tissue that gives the edit room to do exactly that. ‍ A useful rule of thumb: shoot at least three times more B-roll than you think you need. The cost of an extra twenty minutes of crowd shots is essentially zero. The cost of finishing the edit and realizing you have no transition footage is enormous. Composition discipline The signature of an amateur event video is a static, eye-level wide shot of a speaker that remains in place for the entire keynote. The signature of a professional one is a varied composition: high angles, low angles, over-the-shoulder, audience-first, slide-first, hands-on-product. The cuts feel motivated because the framing actually changes. ‍ Mark Campbell Productions frames this as the difference between event videography and event cinematography. Both capture the event. Only the second one tells a story. Audio: The Part Nobody Notices Until It Goes Wrong Bad video gets noticed in passing. Bad audio kills a keynote replay instantly. Ask any seasoned event videographer about their last bad shoot, and you will hear an audio story. Bad video gets noticed in passing. Bad audio kills a keynote replay instantly. ‍ The professional audio chain for an event runs four redundant sources in parallel. First, a direct feed from the venue's audio board, which gives you the cleanest possible signal of every microphone the venue is already running. Second, a wireless lavalier on the speaker as a backup in case the board feed has issues. Third, an on-camera shotgun for ambient room sound (laughter, applause, energy). Fourth, an independent digital recorder rolling the entire session as a fail-safe. ‍ The reason for the redundancy is unforgiving. If the board feed fails halfway through a 45-minute keynote and the lav is the only backup, but it runs out of battery at minute 30, you have lost 15 minutes of irrecoverable audio. The crews who stay employed are the ones who never get into that situation. ‍ A useful shortcut when you are vetting an event videography vendor: ask them what their audio plan is. If the answer is "we use the camera mic," keep looking. Storytelling: Turning Footage Into a Watchable Edit Footage is a raw material. The story is the product. The teams that consistently produce event videos people actually share are working from a story arc, not a chronological timeline. The three-act event recap The default arc most professional editors use for an event recap looks like this. ‍ Act one establishes the setting and the stakes: we hosted an event, and here is who came and what they were here for. ‍ Act two delivers the substance: the keynote moments, the product reveal, the customer reaction, the conversations that mattered. ‍ Act three delivers the emotional payoff: standing ovations, networking energy, attendee testimonials, and a visual sense of an event that worked. ‍ A two-minute recap that follows this structure outperforms a five-minute chronological highlight reel almost every time. Use the audio as the spine The strongest event recaps are usually built around a single anchor audio bed: a CEO line from the keynote, a customer testimonial, or a clip of a speaker delivering the conference's thesis. Editors lock that audio first and cut B-roll to it. The result feels like a cohesive narrative rather than a slideshow with music. Cut for the platform The 90-second LinkedIn version, the 30-second Instagram Reel, and the four-minute YouTube recap are not the same edit at different lengths. There are three different stories. Plan and budget for each one separately rather than treating them as exports of the same master. Live Streaming: The Other Half of Modern Event Videography The stream is often the bigger audience. Cut it like a broadcast, not a Zoom call. A 2026 event video budget that excludes a live stream is an outlier. Hybrid event participation is now standard, and the live stream is increasingly the largest audience for any given event, even when the in-person crowd is the priority. ‍ The live stream stack for a professional event runs in addition to, not instead of, the recorded coverage. A typical setup has a dedicated streaming switcher (ATEM Mini Pro, vMix, or Tricaster) ingesting two to four cameras, a graphics overlay system for lower-thirds and sponsor placements, redundant encoders pushing the stream to YouTube and a private hybrid event platform simultaneously, and a dedicated technician running the broadcast separately from the recording crew. ‍ The strategic case is straightforward. The live stream extends the audience by an order of magnitude in some cases. It generates real-time social moments. It gets clipped into next year's promo reel. And it doubles as the cleanest possible recording of every camera angle, since the streamed mix is itself a finished edit. Distribution and Repurposing: Making the Footage Earn Its Keep The single biggest mistake teams make with event videography is treating the recap reel as the deliverable. The recap reel is the artifact. The system that distributes it is the deliverable. The 12-month repurposing plan A well-managed event video shoot produces enough footage to seed a year of marketing content. Map this out before the shoot, not after. ‍ A useful baseline distribution plan looks something like this: ‍ Week 1 post-event: 90-second sizzle reel as the recap email video, social hero, and sales follow-up attachment. Weeks 2 to 4: Eight to twelve short-form clips, one per week, posted across LinkedIn, Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube Shorts Months 2 to 3: Three keynote replays released as on-demand, gated where appropriate, used in sales enablement and SDR outreach. Months 4 to 6: B-roll inserted into product launch videos, customer story videos, recruiting content, paid social ads, and the next event's promo reel. Months 7 to 12: Highlights resurfaced as anniversary posts, anchor content for the next event's landing page, and case studies featuring on-camera customer interviews. ‍ This is the operating model behind Wistia's finding that event pages produce the highest engagement of any page type. It is not the magic of the page. It is what teams actually do with the footage they put there. Optimize per platform, not per export LinkedIn favors square or vertical, captioned, hooky in the first three seconds. Instagram Reels and TikTok favor vertical, fast cuts, and trending audio. YouTube favors landscape, longer form, and indexed thumbnails. The recap edit gets exported once, and then a separate platform-specific cut is made for each surface. Treating these as the same video kills performance on all of them. ‍ The underlying message we cover in our piece on maximizing social media presence with strong visual content applies to event video as well. The platform shapes the format. Scaling Across Many Events: The Enterprise Problem For most companies, hiring a local event videographer for one event is straightforward. Hiring consistent, brand-aligned, predictable event video coverage for forty events a year across twelve cities is the actual hard problem. This is where the operational difficulty of event videography becomes a strategic decision rather than a vendor decision. Why the in-house model breaks at scale The first instinct most companies have is to build an internal video team. It works at low volume. It breaks at high volume for predictable reasons. Internal teams cannot be in two cities at once, which means events outside their home market get either travel-cost-loaded or skipped. ‍ They also struggle during peak-load periods when 10 events occur in a single quarter. Hiring up the team is expensive at full-time-equivalent rates and creates utilization problems in the off-season. Outsourcing each event individually solves the capacity problem but introduces quality and consistency problems: every videographer brings their own visual style, audio approach, and edit pace. The platform model for event video The model that actually scales is platform-mediated: a centralized brief, brand guidelines, and edit standard that applies to every event, sourced through a network of pre-vetted local videographers who can be dispatched to any market on short notice. ‍ This is exactly the operating model Snappr has built for visual content. The same approach works for event videography. With Snappr, an enterprise team defines the shoot guidelines once (camera setups, edit pace, audio standards, deliverable list, brand bumpers) and then dispatches local crews from Snappr's network into any of the markets where the company runs events. Coverage is consistent. Markets that previously had to be skipped because the in-house team could not fly out are now in scope. Edit standards remain constant because edits occur through a centralized post-production pipeline rather than by the local crew. ‍ We have written about how this approach plays out in adjacent visual content categories. The piece on image quality and consistency as key factors for real estate brands lays out the same operating principle: at enterprise scale, consistency across markets is more valuable than peak quality in any single market. Event videography is the same problem as with a moving subject. Why this matters more in 2026 Event marketing budgets are growing again at the enterprise level, and the Gartner survey covered by Campaign shows events claiming 19.3% of all offline marketing spend. The companies that figure out how to capture every one of those events with a consistent visual standard end the year with a content library that their competitors lack. The companies that do not end the year with a folder full of inconsistent videos from twelve different freelancers. ROI Framework: How to Justify Event Video Spend Internally The hardest part of running an event video program is not producing the content. It is defending the line item to a CFO who wants the spend in dollars and the return in dollars. Here is a framework that holds up in that conversation. Step 1: Calculate the all-in cost per asset Take the total event video spend (crew, edit, deliverables, live stream, post-production tools) and divide by the number of finished assets the shoot produces. A $10,000 event shoot that produces 1 sizzle reel, 10 short-form clips, 3 keynote replays, and a B-roll library has 14 asset units. That is roughly $715 per asset. A $20,000 shoot producing 2 sizzle reels, 20 short clips, 5 keynote replays, and a customer story video is $645 per asset. The bigger shoots are usually cheaper per asset. Step 2: Compare against the alternative production cost Producing one studio-shot 30-second social video typically costs $2,500 to $7,500, including talent, location, and editing. The 30-second clips from an event shoot cost roughly $645 to $1,000 each in our example. Event video is consistently the cheapest way to produce on-brand video content per asset, by a margin of 3x to 5x. Step 3: Layer in the qualitative multipliers Event video has structural advantages that no studio shoot can replicate. The footage is authentic (real customers, real reactions, real product being used). The customers in it have already self-selected as advocates. The keynote moments cannot be recreated in the studio. These are not soft benefits; they are why event video clips outperform polished studio content in every social platform's algorithm. Step 4: Tie it to a measurable outcome Pick one number you would have to defend if pushed: revenue influenced by the recap reel in a 90-day post-event window, pipeline created by the email campaign that featured event video, registration rate for next year's event among recipients who saw the recap, and brand search volume in the weeks after the event. Track that number. Compare events with strong video coverage to events without. The gap is the proof. This is the same operating logic Snappr applies to its own enterprise customers. The asset is not the photo or the video. The asset is the measurable lift in conversion that the photo or the video produces. We covered the same principle in how Renters Warehouse increased inquiries by 10x using professional photography. The math is the same. Only the medium changes. ‍ Trends Shaping Event Videography in 2026 and Beyond Real speakers. Real audience. Real reactions. That's what the algorithm rewards in 2026. The discipline is changing fast. Five trends are worth watching as you plan the next twelve months. Trend 1: Vertical video is now the default deliverable, not the afterthought Three years ago, the recap reel was 16:9 horizontal, and the vertical cut was the optional extra. That has flipped. The dominant social platforms (LinkedIn, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube Shorts) are now vertical-first. According to eMarketer, LinkedIn paid video ads grew 30% year over year, driven by short-form vertical content. Event videographers who shoot with vertical reframing in mind from the capture stage produce dramatically better social cuts than crews who shoot pure 16:9 and try to crop after. Trend 2: AI-assisted editing is now baseline Two years ago, AI in post-production was a novelty. In 2026, it is table stakes. Every professional event video edit now goes through some combination of AI transcription, AI clip identification, AI noise reduction, and AI vertical reframing. The crews that resist this are quietly being underpriced by the ones that do not. Trend 3: Live streaming is becoming part of the base package The 2020 to 2022 hybrid event boom established the live stream as a core deliverable. By 2026, it will be increasingly bundled into event video pricing rather than offered as an add-on. Companies that do not stream their flagship events are now the exception. Trend 4: First-party event content is replacing stock and influencer content Brands are pulling back from stock footage and creator-licensed content in favor of authentic first-party event footage. The customers in your event recap are real customers. The reactions are real reactions. The product demos are real demos. That authenticity is exactly what the algorithms reward in 2026. Trend 5: Event video is becoming a recruiting asset The fastest-growing use case for event videography in 2026 is not marketing, it is recruiting. Talent teams are using customer-event footage and internal-event footage in employer-brand campaigns at every funnel stage. A finished event video that shows a real team and real customers in real rooms now serves double duty as both a sales and a hiring asset. The same pattern shows up in how we have written about the rise of virtual tours for real estate . The visual asset starts in one channel and ends up powering several. The event video has crossed that threshold. Working With Snappr on Event Videography If you have read this far, you already know event videography is more of an operational problem than a creative one. The hard part is not the shoot. The hard part is getting consistent coverage across every event your company runs, in every market, on the schedule dictated by the marketing calendar, with the same brand standard each time. ‍ That is the problem Snappr has built its platform around. Snappr operates the largest on-demand professional visual content network in the world, covering 95% of US geography and 90% of the English-speaking world. Customers include 73% of the Fortune 500. The platform that handles photography for DoorDash, Instacart, and Renters Warehouse is the same platform that handles event video coverage for enterprise marketing teams. ‍ What that looks like in practice for event videography: - One brief, applied to every event, in every city - Pre-vetted local crews dispatched on short notice - Centralized post-production with consistent edit standards - A unified footage library with tagging, search, and API access - Workflow automation that triggers shoots from your event calendar - AI-accelerated editing pipeline for fast post-event turnaround. ‍ If your team runs more than four to six events a year and the in-house or one-off vendor model is straining, the platform model is the path forward. Book time with our Enterprise Visual Partners and hop on a free assessment call to map your event video program against your 2026 calendar. Frequently Asked Questions What is event videography? Event videography is the professional video coverage of corporate, social, and special events, including conferences, product launches, awards ceremonies, fundraisers, panels, concerts, and trade shows. It typically excludes weddings, which are a separate discipline. Event videography produces both real-time deliverables (live streams, day-of social clips) and longer-format assets (recap reels, keynote replays, B-roll libraries) used across marketing, sales, and recruiting. How much does event videography cost in 2026? According to Thumbtack's 2025 videographer cost data, the national average price for a videographer is $961, with the typical range running $900 to $1,025. For a full-day corporate event with a two-person crew and multi-cam edit, expect $1,500 to $5,000. For a three-camera professional crew with dedicated audio and live streaming, $5,000 to $15,000 per event day is the norm. Enterprise event video programs that cover 20-plus events a year typically start at $50,000 annually. What does an event videographer actually deliver? A typical event videography package produces a 60- to 90-second sizzle reel, eight to twelve short-form social clips, full-length recordings of keynote sessions, a B-roll library, and, optionally, a live stream and customer interview content. The exact list of deliverables should be defined before the shoot, not after, because it determines crew size, gear, and the edit budget. How is event videography different from event photography? Event photography produces still images optimized for instant social sharing and post-event recap decks. Event videography produces motion footage optimized for storytelling, social engagement, and long-tail content. They are usually booked together, often from the same vendor, because they share venue access, scheduling, and creative direction. Most enterprise event teams treat them as a single visual content workflow. What event videography services should an enterprise buyer look for? The non-negotiables are multi-camera coverage (three or more), a professional redundant audio chain (board feed plus wireless plus shotgun plus independent recorder), a defined deliverable list before the shoot, a contingency plan for gear and schedule failures, and consistent crew availability across the markets where your events take place. For enterprise buyers running multiple events per year across multiple cities, a network-based platform like Snappr is structurally better than a single freelance vendor. How long does it take to get the final event video? Standard turnaround for a recap reel is 5 to 10 business days post-event. Short-form social clips can be turned around in 24 to 48 hours, particularly with AI-assisted editing pipelines. Full keynote replays are typically delivered within 2 to 3 weeks. Live streams are real-time. Faster turnarounds are possible with rush pricing. Should I hire a local event videographer or work with a national platform? For a single event in a single city, a local event videographer is usually the right call. For more than four events a year, especially across multiple markets, a national platform is structurally better because it solves the consistency, capacity, and travel-cost problems that break local-vendor models at scale. The point at which the platform model wins on cost alone is usually around six events per year. ‍ Sources Campaign — Gartner 2025 CMO Spend Survey — events = 19.3% of offline marketing spend (cited twice: intro + "Why this matters in 2026") DigitalApplied — Wyzowl 2026 video marketing survey — 91% of businesses use video; 86% landing-page conversion lift; 65% email CTR lift Wistia — 2026 State of Video Report — 13M videos / 79M hours; event pages = highest engagement of any page type (cited twice) eMarketer — LinkedIn video ads — LinkedIn paid video ads +30% YoY (cited twice: business case + vertical-video trend) Bull and Wolf — event production guide — "every event has a narrative arc" (B-roll/storytelling) Mark Campbell Productions — Event Videography 101 — videography vs. cinematography (composition) Thumbtack — 2025 videographer cost data — national average $961, range $900–$1,025

title: KYC decision intelligence: Building defensible decisions
summary: In regulated KYC environments, the decision is the artifact that must be defended. Learn why explainability comes from governed workflows, not AI models alone.
body_text: The decision is the regulated artifact Why the decision – not the model, not the data – is the regulated artifact, and why explainability lives in the workflow rather than the algorithm. In Part 1 we argued that the race to onboard faster optimizes the experience while also being the least consequential moment in the client relationship from a regulatory standpoint. The better question is how to make, govern, and evidence risk decisions across the whole lifecycle. That question raises an obvious follow-up: Of everything an institution builds and buys, what is the part that actually has to hold up? Most Know your customer ( KYC ) transformation budgets of the last 10 years went into inputs: more data, more sources, more documents, better screening lists, document-extraction models, beneficial-ownership graphs, perpetual-KYC signal feeds. All useful and needed, though none is the thing actually under supervision. So what is? A regulator does not examine your data lake. An examiner does not grade your model’s AUC – a high AUC tells you a model discriminates well on average, but says nothing about whether you can defend a specific decision about a specific client. What an examiner questions is a decision – why this client was rated high risk and that one was not, why this alert was closed and that SAR was filed, who approved the exception and under which version of which policy. The regulated artifact has always been the decision and its defensibility. Everything else is evidence in service of it. This is the quiet failure in most architectures. Today they are rich in data and models and yet often light in decision explainability and traceability. They can tell you the answer but not reconstruct how the answer was reached – precisely the question that gets asked in an exam, a lookback, or litigation. An institution that cannot reproduce the conditions of a past decision does not really have a control; it has an outcome it hopes was right. And the decision is rarely about a single, tidy entity. The “who” in Know your customer is usually a network: beneficial owners, officers, counterparties, brokers, agents, suppliers, related parties, the layers of a multi-jurisdiction group structure. Risk lives in the relationships between those parties at least as much as in any one of them, and the picture only resolves when you can see all of them together. Multi-country due diligence sharpens the point: the same entity is read against different registries, different ownership-disclosure regimes, different sanctions and tax rules, and different definitions of what even counts as a controlling interest. Assess one node in isolation, through one jurisdiction’s lens, and you are not looking at the real risk – you are looking at a fragment of it and calling it the whole. A financial firm has to hold that whole-network, multi-jurisdiction view, or the decisions it records are confidently wrong. The institutions pulling ahead treat CLM-KYC as a unified system for decisions , not for KYC data. That is a meaningfully different design goal,and very few platforms are actually truly built for it. Explainability is a property of the process, not the model There is a comfortable myth in the industry that you can take a black-box model, bolt on a layer of feature-importance scores, and call the result “explainable AI”. In a regulated KYC context, this is close to meaningless. What an examiner wants is not a heat map of which variables nudged a score. It is the ability to reconstruct the decision in full: the policy in force at the time, the thresholds that applied, the data that was used, who reviewed it, the escalation path it travelled, and – crucially – what the alternative outcomes were and why they were rejected. All of which is recoverable from the workflow the model operated inside. This is the insight that inverts the whole AI conversation. Explainability is not something you extract from a model after the fact. It is something the surrounding process either provides by design or never provides at all. The most perfect model in the world, dropped into an ungoverned path whose output flows straight into action – no record of which policy applied, which thresholds were used, what data it saw, or who approved the result – produces decisions you cannot defend, because nothing around the model ever captured why. A model inside a governed workflow that records all of that produces decisions you can . It matters here that KYC decisions are asymmetric in a way most AI use cases are not. A bad KYC decision can debank a legitimate business, exclude a person from the financial system, or file a suspicious-activity report against someone who will never see it and cannot contest it. The party harmed by an unexplainable wrong decision usually has no recourse. That asymmetry raises the bar far above “accurate enough.” The standard must be defensible , and defensibility is earned in the process, not the model. Next in the series → Knowing the decision must be defensible is one thing; building AI you can actually trust to make or inform it is another. In Part 3 – “Predictable AI, and the operating model that follows” – we get concrete: how to put guardrails around agentic automation, and how a governed lifecycle makes most KYC work simply disappear.

title: How PMIS Technology Is Transforming Transportation Infrastructure Programs
summary: Learn about tailored Transportation PMIS solutions that modernize infrastructure and streamline complex transportation projects.
body_text: Innovation 08-13-2026 How PMIS Technology Is Transforming Transportation Infrastructure Programs Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Email Estimated reading time: 6 minutes Key Takeaways We are using technology and digital solutions to modernize transportation infrastructure, focusing on tailored digital transformation for major programs. Our PMIS services streamline program management by providing a centralized platform that enhances visibility, consistency, and control. iNET® is an advanced management system that leverages AI and ML to enhance the efficiency and safety of transportation networks. How is Parsons using technology and digital solutions to modernize transportation infrastructure? We combine proven program management oversight (PMO) with practical, agency-focused digital transformation that improves how major transportation programs are delivered. We bring not only the ability to implement technology, but also the expertise to align digital tools with the governance, controls, and reporting demands of large, complex capital programs. We focus on turning technology into measurable program value and configure digital solutions to support agency-specific business processes, approval paths, and oversight requirements, helping reduce manual effort, eliminate information silos, improve accountability, and strengthen consistency across the program. Rather than applying a one-size-fits-all system, we deliver a scalable framework tailored to the operational needs of our clients. From transportation to aviation, we’ve been able to modernize infrastructure through advanced digital solutions. Examples of this include our work on the Hudson Tunnel in New York City, where we’ve used technology to manage RFIs and submittals and track cost reporting and change management. Additionally, we’ve implemented digital solutions for various airport improvement projects at the Fort Lauderdale, FL, airport; Fort Myers, FL, airport; Raleigh-Durham, NC, airport; Memphis, TN, airport; and Knoxville, TN, airport. How do Parsons’ PMIS services streamline program management? Our program management information system (PMIS) services can streamline program management for clients by providing a centralized digital platform that improves visibility, consistency, and control across large and complex transportation programs. This service integrates cost, schedule, risk, document management, workflows, and reporting into a single system, reducing reliance on manual processes and disconnected tools. This approach helps clients standardize program controls, accelerate reviews and approvals, improve coordination among agency staff, consultants, and contractors, and provide leadership with real-time insight into program performance. How does PMIS benefit clients? A PMIS benefits clients by providing a single, reliable source of truth for managing program information across the full asset lifecycle. Rather than relying on separate spreadsheets, emails, and standalone tracking tools, PMIS brings together cost, schedule, risk, documents, workflows, and reporting in one centralized platform. This improves data consistency, reduces duplication, and gives clients better visibility into overall program performance. PMIS also helps clients streamline processes and improve efficiency. Routine tasks such as document reviews, approvals, change tracking, invoice processing, and status reporting can be automated through standardized workflows. This reduces manual effort, shortens turnaround times, and helps ensure that processes are followed consistently across projects and stakeholders. A PMIS allows trends to be identified early and corrective action to be taken before problems can grow, creating more proactive program management. As part of our work at Houston Airport, we built out Power BI dashboards and reports that tracked costs and helped implement cost management solutions. It was so successful that the airport’s facilities management group has chosen to implement this technology as part of other larger capital improvement projects. They’re expanding the technology’s functionality at a crawl, walk, run pace so that it is implemented in a phased progression to match growth and overall need. What is iNET® and how is it valuable to clients? iNET® is an advanced transportation management system. By applying state-of-the-art operational solutions and leveraging artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML), iNET® helps improve the management, efficiency, effectiveness, and safety of transportation networks, big or small. Our award-winning advanced traffic management solution is flexible and scalable, designed to meet our clients where they are, regardless of the size of their operations. By integrating data from multiple sources, iNET® creates a “single pane of glass” to help operators quickly identify issues and rectify problems, proactively improving performance for the travelers they serve. What does being a trusted partner mean to Parsons? To us, being a trusted partner means more than delivering technical services; it means working as an extension of the client’s team and consistently acting in the client’s best interest. We build trust through transparency, accountability, responsiveness, and a clear commitment to helping our clients achieve their program goals. Being a trusted partner means listening carefully, understanding the client’s priorities, and aligning our approach with their specific needs, challenges, and objectives. It also means providing honest, informed guidance, identifying risks early, communicating clearly, and bringing forward practical solutions that support sound decision-making. At Parsons, trust is earned by delivering consistent results, maintaining strong stewardship of public resources, and fostering collaboration among all stakeholders. We understand that for agencies managing complex transportation programs, reliability and credibility are essential. Our role is to provide leadership, expertise, and support that help clients move forward with confidence. In practice, being a trusted partner means being committed to: Acting with integrity and professionalism Being proactive rather than reactive Maintaining open and transparent communication Adapting to the client’s needs and operating environment Focusing on long-term value, not just short-term tasks Ultimately, we define a trusted partnership as one built on performance, accountability, and a shared commitment to successful outcomes. title: Red Cat Announces Multiyear Partnership with Washington Commanders to Support America's Military Community
summary: SALT LAKE CITY, Aug. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Red Cat Holdings, Inc. (Nasdaq: RCAT) (“Red Cat” or the “Company”), a…...
body_text: Red Cat Announces Multiyear Partnership with Washington Commanders to Support America's Military Community August 10, 2026 5:58am EDT Download as PDF SALT LAKE CITY, Aug. 10, 2026 (GLOBE NEWSWIRE) -- Red Cat Holdings, Inc . (Nasdaq: RCAT) (“Red Cat” or the “Company”), a U.S.-based provider of advanced all-domain drone and robotic solutions for defense and national security, today announced a multiyear partnership with the Washington Commanders to support U.S. service members, veterans, and their families. As a Proud Partner of the Washington Commanders, Red Cat and the team are working together on military appreciation initiatives, including community events, fan experiences, and recognition programs that honor service members, veterans, and military families throughout the season. The partnership reflects both organizations' commitments to supporting those who serve and highlights Red Cat's mission to strengthen American leadership in autonomous systems. Through its Family of Systems, Red Cat develops secure, American made drone technologies that provide critical intelligence and situational awareness to the U.S. military and allied forces. "Red Cat is focused on building the next generation of autonomous systems for the men and women who defend our country," said Jeff Thompson, Founder and Chief Executive Officer of Red Cat. "Our partnership with the Washington Commanders extends that mission beyond the battlefield by recognizing the service and sacrifice of our military community. We are honored to work alongside an organization that shares our commitment to giving back to those who have given so much." Throughout the upcoming NFL season, Red Cat will launch a comprehensive marketing campaign across one of the country's largest media markets. The partnership will include in-stadium branding and digital signage at Northwest Stadium, military appreciation programming, community initiatives, game day activations, and digital content that highlights Red Cat's commitment to those who serve. "The Washington Commanders are proud to partner with Red Cat to celebrate the military community and the values of service, leadership, and innovation," said Jim Rushton, Chief Partnerships Officer of the Washington Commanders. "Together, we look forward to creating meaningful experiences that recognize our service members while engaging fans throughout the season." About Red Cat Holdings, Inc. Red Cat (Nasdaq: RCAT) is a U.S.-based provider of advanced all-domain drone and robotic solutions for defense and national security. Through its integrated portfolio of trusted U.S. and allied hardware and software, Red Cat supports military, government, and public safety operations across air, land, sea and space. Its systems span small unmanned aircraft systems, uncrewed surface vessels, wireless power transfer technology, and autonomous swarming software to enhance situational awareness, operational effectiveness, and mission safety. Learn more at www.redcat.red . About the Washington Commanders The Washington Commanders, owned by a group led by Managing Partner Josh Harris, were founded in 1932 and are one of the original members of the NFL’s Eastern Division. The team – which plays its home games at Northwest Stadium in Landover, MD and trains at the BigBear.ai Performance Center at Commanders Park in Ashburn, Va. – has won five World Championship titles, including Super Bowls XVII, XXII, and XXVI. The franchise’s storied history has 22 members of the Pro Football Hall of Fame, including multiple Hall of Fame coaches and some of the game’s most accomplished players. The Commanders organization prides itself on positively impacting the DMV through the powerful platform of football, working with numerous community groups, charities, and veteran-focused causes each year. Through the Washington Commanders Foundation, the organization provides support and services to more than 179,000 individuals annually, with a focus on children’s education, health, and wellness.
